endorsements.quote: Under the doctrine, a Data/AI Steering Committee serves as the central coordination and decisionmaking body for AI- and data-related initiatives.
Maintain a continuously updated registry of all candidate and deployed AI tools including deployment status, local owner, intended use, regulatory status, and available system logs
Rely on vendors or departments to declare AI functionality spontaneously, or treat embedded AI features as out of scope.
Classify each tool by data nature and proximity to clinical decision-making before deployment, assigning it to one operational category and to its MDR/AI Act status (Art. 6(1)(b); MDR Rule 11).
This stratification ensures that go vernance intensity is proportionate to actual risk rather than applied uniformly.
Formalized decision gates, managed by the Data/AI Steering Committee, determine progression between phases.
Predefined conditions trigger recalibration, suspension, or withdrawal when performance degrades beyond acceptable thresholds or when contextual changes alter vali dation assumptions.

Once deployed, AI tools are monitored through quantitative and qualitative indicators: adoption and usage patterns, concordance between AI outputs and clinical decisions, user-reported usability, and performance drift detection via statistical monitoring of output distributions .

We propose an institutional AI-related adverse event (AI-AE) reporting system structured around five event categories (Table 2): performance failure, automation bias, workflow disruption, data related incident, and human –AI interaction failure.

Set monitoring indicators, driftdetection thresholds, suspension criteria, and an AI- AE reporting channel with defined escalation to the provider and, where required, competent authorities (Art. 26; Art. 72–73).
(i) end users — intended use, known limitations, expected failure modes, output uncertainty, principles of human–AI interaction;
(iii) institutional leaders and Steering Committ ee members — strategic, ethical, and regulatory dimensions of AI governance, risk –benefit evaluation, and compliance oversight.

We therefore propose that AI competency assessment incorporate structured proficiency testing, analogous to external quality assessment in laboratory medicine or test-case reviews in screening mammography.
Define approved use cases, prohibited uses, data-entry restrictions, validation requirements, and traceability rules for LLM-based tools.

Obtain the intended-use statement, CE marking documentation, MDR certificate where applicable, and postmarket performance data, and verify provider transparency documentation before clinical use (Art. 26; Art. 13).
Define intended purpose, validation, and monitoring; route through the same decision gates as external tools; assess whether development triggers provider/manufacturer obligations.
Deploy research scripts, prototypes, or “internaluse” models in routine care without conformity assessment.
Within this architecture, AI tools undergo staged oversight across pre -deployment assessment, control led deployment, and continuous post-deployment monitoring.
Automate registry updates, version tracking, user access logs, validation reminders, and AI-AE routing through existing ITSM/QMS tools.

It operates as a single point of entry for Data/AI initiatives, bringing together institutional leadership, information systems, the project office, the data prote ction officer, and clinical and medico -technical functions.

unlisted_practices: Inform patients at first contact that their data may be used for AI-based applications and provide a formal opt-out mechanism.
Define explicit institutional AI doctrine establishing principles such as primacy of human clinical judgment and AI as decision support only.
Exclude AI applications that threaten professional autonomy or lack a safe integration pathway or meaningful human oversight.
Develop shared algorithmovigilance databases enabling cross-institutional signal detection.
Standardize AI governance across cancer centers and other clinical institutions through collaboration.

screen.reason: This is a framework/perspective paper presenting an institutional governance framework to operationalize deployer obligations under the EU AI Act.
